items.chName: Unit 3: I’d like to work in the tourist industry
items.text:
Write the direct speech as reported speech.
1) “You should work in the oil industry,” my teacher said to me.
2) “Do you have experience in the area?”, the interviewer asked Faisal.
3) “We should have a meeting to discuss the issue,” Noura said.
4) “How did you forget to check the oil?”, my mum asked my dad.
5) “I won’t stay in student accommodation next year,” I told my mother.
items.ans:
1) My teacher advised me to work in the oil industry.
2) The interviewer asked Faisal whether/if he had experience in the area.
3) Noura suggested having a meeting to discuss the issue.
4) My mum asked my dad how he had managed to forget to check the oil.
5) I told my mother that I wouldn’t stay in student accommodation next year.
steps: Choose the reporting verb that matches the meaning: should → advised / suggested; do you have … ? → asked whether/if; how … ? → asked how.
In reported questions the question form disappears and the verb moves back one tense.

items.text: Put the verbs in brackets into the past simple: 1) Rana (write) … 2) She and Rashid (set up) … 3) They (travel) … 4) They (have) … 5) They (meet) and (sell) … 6) Muna (get) married.
items.ans: 1) wrote  2) set up  3) travelled  4) had  5) met / sold  6) got
steps: past simple of write is wrote and of get is got; both are irregular.
have → had is the past simple used with an object: They had a lot of success.
travelled doubles the final consonant in British spelling.

items.text: When I (meet) her at the airport, Muna (wear) a long blue dress.
items.ans: When I met her at the airport, Muna was wearing a long blue dress.
steps: meeting is a short completed action, so it takes the past simple: met.
wearing describes the situation the moment she met me, so it takes was + wearing.
the action in progress is the background, and the short action interrupts it.
items.title: Worked example: Activity Book C, sentence 4

items.text: Look at the two pictures of a gym, then close the book and make sentences with used to / didn’t use to about the differences.
items.ans: There used to be more people at the gym. / The trainer didn’t use to have a tablet.
steps: One picture shows the past, so the details that have disappeared take didn’t use to.
The other shows today, so the details that appeared take used to (implying they didn’t exist before).

items.text: Play the Had to chain game: the team is “Owner of a restaurant”. Student A: Last week, I had to go to the market with the chef. Student B: …and I had to order a new fridge. Student C: …and I had to interview two waiters.
items.ans: Last week, I had to go to the market with the chef, I had to order a new fridge and I had to interview two waiters.
steps: had to + base verb expresses a past duty in that job.
Each student repeats the previous chain and adds one new item, so the chain grows.
The past of have to is had to with no change in the verb form.

items.text: Find the mistake and rewrite each sentence: 1) We played football when it started to rain, and we had to stop. 2) This gym used to had the best equipment in town. 3) Amjed didn’t used to work out. 4) My brothers and I have help my parents with the housework. 5) If only you told me about your problem before. I could have helped you.
items.ans: 1) We were playing football when it started to rain…  2) This gym used to have…  3) Amjed didn’t use to work out…  4) …have helped…  5) If only you had told me…
steps: Sentence 1 needs the past continuous for the action in progress that was interrupted.
Sentence 2: used to is followed by the base verb have, not had.
Sentence 3: after didn’t we write use without the letter d.
Sentence 4: have/has is followed by the past participle.
Sentence 5: an unreal past regret needs had told, not told.

items.text: Complete each word with the right ending: fract…, ineffic…, unfortun…, independ…, unusu…, identi…, super…, wit…, applica…, discour….
items.ans: fracture, inefficient, unfortunate, independent, unusual, identify, supervise, witness, application, discourage
steps: Note that -ient and -al change the spelling: inefficient, unusual.
Identify ends in -fy, and supervise ends in -vise, not -vice.

items.text: Write true sentences with never about you, your family and your friends: 1) a game (play) 2) food (eat / try / make) 3) a place (be to / visit) 4) a sport or activity (do / run).
items.ans: 1) I’ve never played that game.  2) I’ve never tried / made that food.  3) I’ve never been to that place.  4) I’ve never done that sport.
steps: The structure is subject + have / has + never + past participle.
A past participle is needed after never: played, tried, made, been, done.
The example in the book is: My sister has never held a scorpion.

items.text: For each situation write a question and then a suitable answer using since or for: 1) You have a friend who is learning Japanese. (how long / learn / Japanese?) 2) You meet somebody who is a writer. (how long / write?) 3) You are going to meet a friend of your cousin. (how long / know?)
items.ans: 1) How long has he been learning Japanese? — For two years.  2) How long has he been writing? — Since he was ten.  3) How long have you known him? — For ages.
steps: Learning, writing and knowing all describe activities or states that started in the past and continue now.
Use the present perfect simple for states (know) and the present perfect continuous for activities (learn, write).
Answer with for a period and since a point.

items.text: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning, putting the verbs in brackets in the present perfect simple: 1) We first met them in July. (know) 2) He bought that motorbike a long time ago. (have) 3) She last went to the dentist in September. (not be)
items.ans: 1) We haven’t known them since July.  2) He hasn’t had that motorbike for a long time.  3) She hasn’t been to the dentist since September.
steps: The last time / first / long ago point to a past moment that is still relevant now, so the present perfect is required.
Use since with a point in time (July, September) and for with a period (a long time).
The present participle of have is had, so the form is hasn’t had.

items.text: Complete the sentences with who, which, where or whose and add commas: 1) Riverside Cinema … 2) Beirut … 3) My cousin Mike … 4) My sister … 5) Fatima … 6) The school … 7) My neighbour … 8) The film …
items.ans: 1) …, where …, 2) …, which …, 3) …, who …, 4) …, whose …, 5) …, whose …, 6) where … (no commas), 7) …, whose …, 8) which … (no commas)
steps: Use where for places, who for people, whose for possession.
Add commas only when the clause is non-defining, that is, when it adds extra information.
that is not allowed in a non-defining clause, so sentences 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 take who / which / whose / where, never that.

items.text: Write an essay of 100–120 words with the title “The future of tourism in Iraq”, including the topics accommodation, public transport, types of holidays, tours and your own topic, and using connectors from Exercise C.
items.ans: A strong answer opens with a topic sentence, develops each idea with connectors such as such as / in addition, presents a contrasting point with however or although, and closes with consequently or for this reason.
steps: Start with “Tourism in Iraq is going to grow rapidly in the coming years.”
Use one paragraph for the positive ideas and one for the problem, then a conclusion.
Use at least four connectors from the table: also, as well as, too, in addition, although, but, however, for instance, such as, consequently, for this reason, so.
Close with a recommendation, not just a summary.
